passportName.title: Korean Passport Name Romanizer
passportName.subtitle: Turn a Korean name into Roman letters using the personal-name rules of the Revised Romanization of Korean, and check common surname spellings, airline ticket format and the passport MRZ line.

input.title: Enter the name
input.surnameHint: Two-syllable surnames such as 남궁, 제갈, 선우 or 황보 go in as two syllables.
input.surnameErr: Enter a Hangul surname of 1–{max} syllables.
input.givenHint: Use the Hangul name exactly as registered in the family relation register.
input.givenErr: Enter a Hangul given name of 1–{max} syllables without spaces.
input.styleHint: Writing the syllables together is the rule, and a hyphen between syllables is allowed. Once chosen, the same style is used when the passport is renewed.
input.spellingHint: The first option follows the Revised Romanization; the others are customary spellings often seen on passports.
input.spellingNone: Only the Revised Romanization spelling is shown for this surname. If your family already uses a spelling, check that one too.

result.label: Passport name
result.keepLast: While you are editing, the last valid name is shown.
result.custom: {v} differs from the standard spelling {std} but is commonly used on passports. Once chosen, the same spelling is kept at renewal, so match it with your family's spelling.
result.ll: The name has 'ㄹㄹ' in a row, written as ll under the romanization rules (e.g. 울릉 Ulleung).
result.single: One-letter spellings such as I, O or A can cause trouble with airline bookings or immigration. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs may accept this as a reason to change the spelling.
result.negative: {words} is listed by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs as an example of a spelling with a negative meaning in English. Such spellings can later be a reason for change, so think it over when choosing.
result.ticketHint: Booking forms usually split surname and given name and take the passport spelling without hyphens or spaces. Follow the airline's booking instructions.
result.mrzHint: A 44-character example for a multiple-entry passport (document type PM). Surname and given names are separated by <<, and hyphens or spaces become <. The second line (passport number, birth date, etc.) is omitted.
result.mrzCut: The name is longer than 44 characters, so the rest is cut off. Real passports shorten it under the international standard.
result.copyFailed: Couldn't copy. Press and hold the text to copy it yourself.
result.disclaimer: An example based on the Revised Romanization of Korean and the Passport Act enforcement rules. The actual passport spelling is fixed by what you write on the passport application.

keep.title: Before you decide on a passport name
items: If you already have a passport, keep its romanized name. The same spelling is the rule at renewal, and it can only be changed for reasons set by law.
The name on an airline ticket must match the passport letter for letter. A mismatch can cause problems at check-in or immigration.
For a first passport, think about your family's surname spelling and the name you will use at schools or companies abroad.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs notes that even a lawful change can make a passport look forged when you revisit a country you travelled to before.

share.label: Passport name example
share.privacy: The shared link and image include the name you entered. Check before sending it to others.

rules.title: Name rules in the Revised Romanization
items: Write the surname first and the given name after a space. The given name is written as one word, and a hyphen between syllables is allowed. Example: 민용하 Min Yongha (Min Yong-ha)
Sound changes inside a given name are not reflected. 한복남 is Han Boknam even though it sounds like 'Bongnam', and 홍빛나 is Hong Bitna. That is why this tool converts each syllable separately.
Final ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ are written k, t, p (복 bok, 빛 bit). 'ㄹ' is r before a vowel, l as a final, and 'ㄹㄹ' is ll.
'ㅢ' is written ui even when it sounds like 'ㅣ' (희 hui).
The rules say surnames are 'to be set separately', and no standard has been fixed yet. That is why many passports use long-standing customary spellings.

Passports romanize the Hangul name in the family relation register syllable by syllable (Passport Act Enforcement Rules, Article 2-2). A foreign-style name with the same sound, such as KIM ESTHER for 김에스더, is allowed.

change.title: When an existing passport name can be changed
items: When it clearly differs from the Korean pronunciation. A spelling that follows the romanization rules, or one used by 50% or more or by 10,000 or more people with the same Hangul surname or name, cannot be changed (MOFA Notice 2024-10; given names are judged by syllable).

When you have used another spelling for work or study abroad and not changing it would seriously affect your stay or activities. Proof of employment or enrolment is needed; language test scores alone are not enough.
When family members travel together and need to show they are family, only the surname can be matched to the family. The given name cannot be changed.
Adding, changing or removing a spouse's surname ('spouse of' format), a spelling listed in dictionaries with a negative meaning, or a legal change of the Hangul name.
A first-ever passport that has not been used for any border crossing, or once after age 18 for a spelling chosen before 18 and used since.
Matching an emigration visa, someone with the same name being barred from entry, or other cases accepted by the Minister of Foreign Affairs (Passport Act Enforcement Decree, Article 3-2(2)).

tips.title: Check before you decide
items: If you have an old passport, look at its romanized name first. Using the same spelling is the rule.
Check how your family spells the surname. For a child's first passport, matching the parents' spelling makes it easier to show you are a family at immigration.
If you already hold a foreign visa, changing the spelling may cause problems with it, so tell the officer when you apply.
Titles, honorifics, numbers, symbols (DR, SIR, 1ST, etc.) and baptismal names cannot be part of a passport name.
Book flights with the passport spelling and check that surname and given name are not swapped before paying.

surnames.title: Spellings of common surnames
surnames.desc: Shows the Revised Romanization spelling together with customary spellings recorded as in actual use by the National Institute of Korean Language that are still common today. The order is not a usage ranking.

items.q: Should 이 be written LEE or I?
items.a: The romanization rules give I, but no standard has been set for surnames, so customary spellings such as LEE, YI and RHEE are common on passports. If your family already uses a spelling, matching it makes border checks easier.

items.q: Should the given name be joined or hyphenated?
items.a: Joining is the rule, and a hyphen between syllables (GIL-DONG) is allowed. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs says a space is also allowed on request, but the style you choose is kept at renewal.

items.q: Can I change my passport name later?
items.a: In principle it is hard. It can only be changed for reasons set in the Passport Act Enforcement Decree (pronunciation mismatch, long use abroad, matching the family surname, a legal name change, once after age 18, etc.). It is not a way to switch to a spelling you prefer.

items.q: What if my airline ticket name differs slightly from my passport?
items.a: Airlines require the same name as the passport. A different spelling can lead to denied boarding or a name-correction fee, so check it letter by letter when booking. Correction rules vary by airline.

items.q: Why is 빛나 BITNA and not BINNA?
items.a: The romanization rules do not reflect sound changes inside a given name. The official example writes 홍빛나 as Hong Bitna. So the tool shows each syllable converted separately.

It is the two-line machine readable zone under the photo page. Under the ICAO standard it lists surname<<given names, fills gaps with < and makes each line 44 characters. Border control machines read it, so it uses the same spelling as your passport name.

items.q: Can a foreign-style name (e.g. 에스더) be written in its English spelling?
items.a: If it sounds the same as the Hangul name in the family relation register, it can be written like KIM ESTHER. This tool shows the standard romanization (ESEUDEO), so check the foreign spelling separately when you apply.

sources.title: Basis and sources
sources.rr: National Institute of Korean Language, Revised Romanization of Korean (MCST Notice 2014-42, 2014-12-05) — Chapter 3 Article 4 personal names, Chapter 2 tables
sources.rule: Korea Law Information Center, Passport Act Enforcement Rules Article 2-2 — romanized name and changes
sources.decree: Korea Law Information Center, Passport Act Enforcement Decree Article 3-2 (version in force from 2026-03-01) — reasons for change
sources.notice: MOFA Notice 2024-10 (2024-12-31) — spellings used by 50% or 10,000+ people cannot be changed
sources.basic: MOFA Passport portal, basic rules for romanized names
sources.change: MOFA Passport portal, requirements for changing romanized names
sources.nikl1991: National Institute of Korean Language, Saegugeosaenghwal Spring 1991, Seo Jeong-su, 'On romanizing Korean names' — surname spellings in actual use
sources.method: Given names are converted syllable by syllable using the romanization tables (finals k, t, p; ㄹㄹ as ll). For surnames the standard spelling is shown with customary options. The MRZ is an example of the first 44-character line of the ICAO Doc 9303 passport format (TD3). Surname options are not listed by usage share.
sources.asOf: Checked {date}. Passport rules can change, so check the MOFA passport portal before applying.
